analogy.p: Think of the cathode as a gate that lets out only the 'least stubborn' passenger. Metal ions and H⁺ ions are queuing to take electrons; the one that is least reluctant to become an atom (the less reactive element) goes first, while the stubborn one (a very reactive metal) stays as an ion in the crowd. At the anode, halide ions are 'first in line' to give up electrons, but if there are none, OH⁻ steps up. The analogy breaks down because ions do not make choices: the outcome is decided by how easily each is discharged under the conditions.
analogy.t: A school exit with two doors

bullets: **Aqueous solution** = ionic compound dissolved in water.
Water ionises to a very small extent: **H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻**, so every aqueous solution contains **H⁺ and OH⁻**.
The **positive ions** present are the metal ion and **H⁺**; both are attracted to the **cathode**.
The **negative ions** present are the non-metal ion and **OH⁻**; both are attracted to the **anode**.
Only **one product** forms at each electrode: the ion that is more easily discharged.
This is why the products of an aqueous solution can differ from the molten compound (e.g. NaCl(l) gives sodium, NaCl(aq) gives hydrogen).
The ions that are **not** discharged stay in the solution.
core.p: In **molten** electrolysis the only ions present come from the compound, so the products are easy to predict. In an **aqueous solution** (a compound dissolved in water) there are more ions, because **water itself ionises slightly** to give hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions: H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻. There are therefore **four** types of ion in the electrolyte: two from the dissolved compound and two from the water. At each electrode only **one** ion is discharged, so you must decide which of the two competing ions wins. The overall result depends on the position of the metal in the reactivity series and on whether a halide is present.

bullets: Metal **more reactive** than hydrogen (e.g. potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium): **hydrogen** is produced.
Metal **less reactive** than hydrogen (e.g. copper, silver, gold): the **metal** is produced.
Hydrogen half equation: **2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂** (reduction).
Metal half equation: e.g. **Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu**, **Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag**.
The reactive metal ions (Na⁺, K⁺) are left in solution.
Observation: **bubbles of colourless gas** (hydrogen) or a **solid deposit** (copper is pink-brown/orange-brown) on the cathode.
The metal formed at the cathode is a **solid** that deposits on the electrode (not molten as in molten electrolysis).
core.p: At the cathode, the competition is between the **metal ion** and the **hydrogen ion**. If the metal is **more reactive than hydrogen**, the metal stays as ions in the solution and **hydrogen gas** is produced. If the metal is **less reactive than hydrogen**, the metal ions are discharged and the **metal** is produced. In other words, the less reactive element is the one that is more willing to gain electrons and become an atom.

bullets: Halide present (Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻): **halogen** produced: **Cl₂, Br₂, I₂**.
No halide (e.g. sulfate or nitrate solutions): **oxygen** is produced from OH⁻.
Oxygen half equation (Higher tier): **4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻**.
Chlorine half equation: **2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻** (similarly 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻, 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻).
Observation: bubbles of **colourless oxygen**, **pale green chlorine**, or a **brown bromine/iodine colour** in solution near the anode.
Oxidation occurs at the anode because ions **lose electrons**.
Sulfate and nitrate ions stay in solution.
core.p: At the anode, the competition is between the **non-metal ion** and the **hydroxide ion**. If the solution contains a **halide ion** (chloride, bromide or iodide), the **halogen** (chlorine, bromine or iodine) is produced. If there is no halide ion, **hydroxide ions** are discharged and **oxygen** is produced. Ions such as sulfate (SO₄²⁻) and nitrate (NO₃⁻) are never discharged in this course; instead hydroxide ions lose electrons and form oxygen and water.

bullets: **More reactive** element = prefers to stay as an **ion** in solution.
**Less reactive** element = more easily **discharged** to form atoms.
Hydrogen is placed in the reactivity series below the common metals such as zinc, iron and lead but above copper, and is used as the dividing line in this topic.
So Na⁺, K⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺ stay in solution while H⁺ is discharged.
So Cu²⁺ and Ag⁺ are discharged, while H⁺ stays in solution.
Learn the rule as given: the exam uses metals clearly above hydrogen (e.g. sodium, potassium) or clearly below hydrogen (copper, silver).
This is the same idea as **displacement**: the less reactive element is easier to release.
core.h: Why hydrogen is made if the metal is reactive
core.p: The reactivity series tells us how readily metals form positive ions. A very reactive metal, such as sodium, holds on strongly to its positive charge and has a strong tendency to remain as an ion in solution. Hydrogen is much less reactive than sodium, so the hydrogen ions from water are discharged first at the cathode. For a metal such as copper, which is less reactive than hydrogen, the copper ions are the ones more easily reduced, so copper forms. This idea links directly to the reactivity series.

bullets: Cathode: **2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂** (bubbles of hydrogen; squeaky pop).
Anode: **2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻** (chlorine; bleaches damp litmus paper).
Left in solution: **Na⁺ and OH⁻**, i.e. aqueous sodium hydroxide (the solution becomes alkaline).
Overall: 2NaCl(aq) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g) + Cl₂(g).
Contrast with **molten** NaCl, which gives sodium metal and chlorine.
Uses: chlorine (bleach, water treatment), sodium hydroxide (soap, paper), hydrogen (fuel, making ammonia).
Chlorine is toxic, so collect it carefully in a fume cupboard.
core.p: Sodium chloride solution contains Na⁺, Cl⁻, H⁺ and OH⁻ ions. At the **cathode**, sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so **hydrogen** gas is produced. At the **anode**, a halide (chloride) is present, so **chlorine** gas is produced. The ions left in solution are **Na⁺ and OH⁻**, so the solution becomes **sodium hydroxide**, an alkali. This process is an important industrial one because it makes three useful products: hydrogen, chlorine and sodium hydroxide.

bullets: Cathode: **Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu**: a **pink/orange-brown solid** coats the electrode.
Anode: **4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻**: bubbles of colourless oxygen.
The solution **loses its blue colour** gradually as Cu²⁺ ions are removed (it stays blue only while copper ions remain).
Sulfate ions are not discharged and stay in the solution.
Oxygen can be tested: it **relights a glowing splint**.
With graphite (inert) electrodes the electrodes do not change; only the copper deposit forms on the cathode.
Copper sulfate is harmful, so avoid contact and wear eye protection.
core.p: Copper(II) sulfate solution contains Cu²⁺, SO₄²⁻, H⁺ and OH⁻ ions. At the **cathode**, copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so **copper metal** is deposited. At the **anode**, there is no halide, so **hydroxide ions** are discharged and **oxygen** is produced. As copper ions are used up, the **blue colour of the solution fades**. This is a good example for a required practical because you can see the copper forming and the bubbles of oxygen.

bullets: Cathode: **2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂**.
Anode: **4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻**.
Overall: **2H₂O(l) → 2H₂(g) + O₂(g)**.
Volume ratio **H₂ : O₂ = 2 : 1** (same temperature and pressure).
Pure water barely conducts as it has very few ions, so acid (or a soluble salt like sodium sulfate) is added.
The same products (H₂ and O₂) form for sodium sulfate or sodium hydroxide solution.
The concentration of acid rises slowly as water is used up.
core.h: Electrolysis of dilute sulfuric acid and water
core.p: Dilute sulfuric acid contains H⁺, SO₄²⁻, and OH⁻ (from water). At the **cathode**, the only positive ion is H⁺, so **hydrogen** is made. At the **anode**, there is no halide, so **oxygen** is made. Overall, water is being decomposed: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂. The volume of hydrogen collected is **twice** the volume of oxygen, because each oxygen molecule releases 4 electrons but each hydrogen molecule uses only 2. The acid is only there to supply ions so that the water can conduct.

bullets: **Step 1**: pour about 50 cm³ of the solution into a beaker (or a suitable container).
**Step 2**: place two **graphite electrodes** in the solution, held apart, not touching.
**Step 3**: connect the electrodes to a **d.c. supply** with leads and crocodile clips.
**Step 4**: switch on and record observations at each electrode (bubbles, colour, deposit).
**Step 5**: test any gas: hydrogen (squeaky pop), oxygen (relights glowing splint), chlorine (bleaches damp litmus paper).
**Step 6**: switch off, rinse electrodes, and repeat with a different solution.
Record results in a table: solution, ions present, observation at cathode, observation at anode, product identified.
core.p: In the required practical you investigate what happens when aqueous solutions are electrolysed using **inert electrodes**, and test the hypothesis that the products depend on the ions present. Use solutions such as copper(II) chloride, sodium chloride, sodium sulfate and dilute sulfuric acid. Work with a low-voltage **d.c.** supply (about 4 to 6 V). Place the electrodes in the solution so that they do not touch, connect them with crocodile clips, switch on, and watch each electrode. Test any gas collected using the standard gas tests.

bullets: Independent variable: **type of solution (ions present)**.
Dependent variable: **products formed at each electrode**.
Control variables: **voltage, concentration, volume, electrodes, time**.
Hypothesis: link the **reactivity of the metal** to whether H₂ or the metal forms; link **halides** to halogen production.
Safety: wear **eye protection**; work in a **fume cupboard** or well-ventilated area if chlorine may form; use **low concentrations**.
Do not let the electrodes touch (this would cause a short circuit); keep leads away from water.
Repeat for reliability; use damp litmus paper and splint tests to **identify** the gases.
core.p: A good investigation changes one variable and controls the others. The **independent variable** is the **solution** (and therefore the ions present). The **dependent variable** is the **product at each electrode**. **Control variables** include the voltage, the concentration and volume of solution, the electrode material and the time. A suitable **hypothesis** is, for example, 'if the metal in the solution is more reactive than hydrogen, then hydrogen will be produced at the cathode'. Safety matters because some products are hazardous.

bullets: Step 1: list the four ions (compound ions + **H⁺, OH⁻**).
Step 2: **cathode**: metal below hydrogen → metal; metal above hydrogen → **H₂**.
Step 3: **anode**: halide present → **halogen**; otherwise **O₂**.
Step 4: say what ions are left in the solution (e.g. Na⁺ and OH⁻ → NaOH).
Example: KBr(aq): cathode H₂, anode Br₂ (brown), left K⁺ and OH⁻.
Example: AgNO₃(aq): cathode Ag, anode O₂.
Always check you have named **one product at each electrode**.
core.p: For any aqueous ionic compound, follow the same method. First, write down the ions in the compound and add H⁺ and OH⁻. Then pick the cathode product using the reactivity of the metal compared with hydrogen. Next pick the anode product by checking for a halide. State the products and any change to the solution. This approach works for unfamiliar compounds because it is based on rules rather than memory.

bullets: **Molten vs aqueous**: molten has only the compound's ions; aqueous also has **H⁺ and OH⁻**.
**Half equations** (HT): 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂; 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻; 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻; Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu.
Electron balance: 4e⁻ produce 2H₂ at the cathode and 1 O₂ at the anode → ratio **2 : 1**.
Link to **gas tests**: hydrogen pop, oxygen relights splint, chlorine bleaches damp litmus.
Link to **reactivity series**: decides whether hydrogen or the metal forms.
Link to **industry**: chlor-alkali process from brine.
Link to **acids and alkalis**: sodium hydroxide formed raises the pH of the solution.
core.p: This topic builds on ionic bonding, the reactivity series, and oxidation and reduction. It also links to **energy**, because electricity drives the reaction, and to **tests for gases** in the chemical analysis topic. At Higher tier you need to **write half equations** for the electrode reactions, including 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ and 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂, and to understand the 2:1 hydrogen to oxygen volume ratio from electron balance. You should also be able to compare electrolysis of molten and aqueous compounds.

exam: Command words: **Predict** (use the rules to state products), **Explain** (use ions and 'because'), **Describe** (observations at each electrode), **Write a half equation** (balance charge, electrons on the correct side).
Always state **which ions are present**, including **H⁺ and OH⁻** from water, in 'explain' questions.
For the cathode: compare the **reactivity of the metal with hydrogen**; 'sodium is more reactive than hydrogen so hydrogen is produced'.
For the anode: say whether a **halide is present**; if not, oxygen from hydroxide ions.
Half equations (2 marks): correct species and correct electrons/charge; typical ones to learn are 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂, 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻, 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.
Required practical questions often ask for the **independent, dependent and control variables**, a **hypothesis**, **safety precautions**, or how to **test the gases**.
Give the **test and result** for each gas: hydrogen (lit splint, squeaky pop), oxygen (glowing splint relights), chlorine (damp litmus paper bleached).
For data questions, identify patterns: e.g. all sodium, potassium solutions give hydrogen at the cathode.
For a 6 mark question, include: ions present, which move to each electrode, which is discharged and why, half equations, products and observations, what remains in solution.
Don't confuse molten and aqueous: check whether the question says '(l)' or '(aq)' or 'solution'.

mistakes.r: Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen is formed at the cathode; sodium would only form from molten NaCl.
mistakes.w: Sodium is formed at the cathode when sodium chloride solution is electrolysed.

mistakes.r: Oxygen comes from hydroxide ions (from water): 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻.
mistakes.w: Oxygen comes from the sulfate ions.

mistakes.r: Every aqueous solution contains H⁺ and OH⁻ from water, and they compete at the electrodes.
mistakes.w: Forgetting the H⁺ and OH⁻ ions from water.

mistakes.r: Chlorine forms at the anode (positive electrode), where chloride ions lose electrons.
mistakes.w: Chlorine is made at the cathode.

mistakes.r: Na⁺ and OH⁻ remain, so sodium hydroxide solution is formed (the solution becomes alkaline).
mistakes.w: The solution has no ions left after electrolysis of brine.

mistakes.r: Hydrogen is a diatomic gas: write H₂ (and Cl₂, O₂ etc.).
mistakes.w: Writing H instead of H₂ for the hydrogen product.

mistakes.r: A direct (d.c.) supply is needed so that one electrode stays the cathode and one the anode.
mistakes.w: Using an alternating current for electrolysis.

mistakes.r: The blue fades as Cu²⁺ ions are discharged and removed from the solution.
mistakes.w: The blue colour of copper sulfate stays the same.

summary: You must be able to predict and explain the products of electrolysis of aqueous solutions using inert electrodes: hydrogen or the metal at the cathode (depending on reactivity) and a halogen or oxygen at the anode (depending on whether a halide is present), write the half equations at Higher tier, and carry out and evaluate the required practical. It matters because it shows how water's ions change the outcome compared with molten electrolysis.

terms.d: A solution in which a substance is dissolved in water.
A molten or dissolved ionic compound that conducts electricity and is decomposed.
An electrode that does not react with the electrolyte or products, e.g. graphite or platinum.
The positive electrode, where negative ions lose electrons (oxidation).
The negative electrode, where positive ions gain electrons (reduction).
Positive ion present in all aqueous solutions from the ionisation of water; discharged at the cathode if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen.
Negative ion present in all aqueous solutions; discharged at the anode to form oxygen when no halide is present.
A negative ion of a halogen: chloride (Cl⁻), bromide (Br⁻) or iodide (I⁻).
A Group 7 element; diatomic molecules such as Cl₂, Br₂, I₂ are formed at the anode from halide ions.
An ion gains or loses electrons at an electrode to become an uncharged atom or molecule.
Gain of electrons; occurs at the cathode.
Loss of electrons; occurs at the anode.
An equation for one electrode reaction showing electrons, balanced for atoms and charge.
A list of metals in order of reactivity, used to decide whether hydrogen or the metal forms at the cathode.
A testable prediction, often written as 'if ... then ...', that an investigation is designed to test.
Current flowing in one direction only, keeping the electrodes' charges fixed.

worked.ans: 20 cm³ of oxygen, because the ratio of H₂ to O₂ is 2 : 1 (each O₂ releases 4 electrons, each H₂ uses 2).
worked.q: Electrolysis of dilute sulfuric acid collects 40 cm³ of hydrogen at the cathode. What volume of oxygen is collected at the anode? Explain your answer. (3 marks)
steps: Ratio of hydrogen to oxygen molecules is 2 : 1.
Gases at the same temperature and pressure have volumes in the same ratio as moles.

worked.ans: Hydrogen is produced at the cathode because sodium is more reactive than hydrogen; chlorine is produced at the anode because chloride ions are present. Na⁺ and OH⁻ ions remain, so the solution becomes sodium hydroxide, an alkali.
worked.q: Sodium chloride solution is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Describe and explain what is produced at each electrode and what remains in the solution. (6 marks)
steps: Ions present: Na⁺, Cl⁻ (compound) and H⁺, OH⁻ (water).
Cathode: Na⁺ and H⁺ attracted; sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so H⁺ is discharged: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ (hydrogen gas).
Anode: Cl⁻ and OH⁻ attracted; a halide is present, so chloride is discharged: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ (chlorine gas).

worked.ans: Cathode: pink-brown copper solid forms, Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. Anode: bubbles of oxygen. The blue colour of the solution fades as copper ions are used up.
worked.q: Copper(II) sulfate solution is electrolysed using graphite electrodes. State what you would see at each electrode and what happens to the colour of the solution, and write the cathode half equation. (4 marks)
steps: Cathode: copper is less reactive than hydrogen so Cu²⁺ is discharged: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu; a pink/orange-brown solid is seen.
Anode: no halide, so OH⁻ is discharged: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻; bubbles of colourless gas (oxygen).
Cu²⁺ ions are removed from solution, so the blue colour fades.
